## Learning objectives

By the end of this workshop, you will be able to:

1.  Describe at least four methods researchers use to measure balance during walking — including step placement predictability, angular momentum regulation, margin of stability, and center-of-mass displacement — and explain why perturbation experiments are important for studying balance effectively.

2.  Explain how ankle exoskeleton assistance can be timed to improve standing balance recovery, and describe the role of whole-body center-of-mass-level control in balance, as distinct from purely local ankle reflexes.

3.  Distinguish between stability (how quickly a system returns to a steady movement pattern after an unexpected perturbation) and agility (how quickly a system transitions to a new movement target on purpose), and understand how both can be defined and measured using energy-based metrics.

## Overview

### Evaluating Balance Metrics: A Systematic Comparison

A paper from Steve Collins' lab at Stanford used a rigorous experimental design to test how well six commonly used balance metrics actually detect imbalance. The study applied two types of challenges simultaneously: large-scale perturbations using a multi-directional cable system called the "Bump'em" (attached to participants' trunks during treadmill walking), and steady disruptions to the physiological systems that normally support balance — blocking vision, locking the ankles, and using pneumatic air jets fired at the swing leg to disturb foot placement. Ten subjects completed the protocol. The six metrics tested were: step width, step time, step placement predictability, Lyapunov exponent, margin of stability, and center-of-mass displacement. Performance varied substantially across metrics. Foot placement predictability outperformed all other measures globally, while center-of-mass displacement alone performed no better than chance at detecting whether a person was in an unbalanced state.

### Step Placement Predictability

The step placement predictability framework is built on the observation that at mid-stance, a person's center-of-mass position and velocity can be used in a simple linear map to predict where the next footfall will land. This strong linear relationship between mid-stance center-of-mass state and subsequent foot placement suggests that a complex, nonlinear locomotion system may use a relatively simple control rule to regulate balance. The fact that this metric also came out on top in the Collins lab's systematic comparison provides two lines of evidence supporting it as a useful measure of balance control.

### Angular Momentum as a Balance Measure

Whole-body angular momentum is another important balance measure. From a physics standpoint, keeping angular momentum near zero on average prevents a person from pitching forward to the ground; angular momentum represents the combined rotational contributions of all body segments. Ground reaction forces produce moments around the body's center of mass that continually regulate this quantity. Work by Anne Silverman showed that even during steady walking (without perturbations), populations at higher fall risk differ measurably in how they regulate angular momentum. For example, amputees show larger-amplitude swings in frontal-plane angular momentum compared to non-amputees, with the difference most pronounced at slow walking speeds. This suggests that frontal-plane angular momentum fluctuation during steady gait may serve as a useful marker of balance impairment. Studying angular momentum only during steady walking is limited, however; understanding balance fully requires also examining how angular momentum responds to large-scale perturbations.

### Perturbation Experiments and Exoskeleton Assistance

Several perturbation paradigms can be used to study balance beyond steady-state walking. One uses the "Karen" system — a treadmill mounted on a Stewart platform — to deliver phase-locked surface perturbations during walking across 96 combinations of magnitude, direction, and gait phase. Whole-body angular momentum is tracked before, during, and after each perturbation to assess how well the person's system returns to its steady pattern; the recovery process typically spans multiple steps. Another paradigm uses treadmill belt slips timed to either early or late stance, which either inject or remove mechanical energy from the leg. After a belt slip, the contralateral knee's next step appears to be the primary joint compensating for the energy change. A passive hip spring exoskeleton tested in this paradigm did not significantly reduce deviations in angular momentum or mechanical energy following the perturbation, possibly because a passive spring cannot modulate mechanical work with optimal timing.

In a standing balance exoskeleton study conducted in collaboration with Dr. Lena Ting, an ankle exoskeleton was programmed to apply plantar flexion torque faster than the human nervous system's own response latency in reaction to a backward surface perturbation. Balance was measured using a psychometric curve approach: perturbation size was progressively increased until participants took a protective step, identifying the size at which stepping occurred more than 50% of the time. Only the condition in which the exoskeleton acted faster than the human's own response improved this threshold. EMG and ultrasound data further showed that in the fast exoskeleton condition, calf muscle stretch was reduced — yet balance still improved. This suggests that the improvement did not rely on enhanced local ankle reflexes but on a global center-of-mass-level strategy in which information from across the body is integrated to coordinate the balance response.

### Defining Stability and Agility Through Energy and Limit Cycles

A conceptual framework for defining and measuring both stability and agility uses a simple model of rhythmic movement. The experimental platform is a motorized ankle dynamometer: participants lie prone on a table, and their plantar flexors perform a cyclical task that feels like vertical bouncing against a gravitational load, even though only the ankle joint is involved. Participants follow a metronome and aim to maintain a target peak ankle angle. The resulting movement can be represented as a limit cycle in a phase portrait (joint angle vs. angular velocity), and the total mechanical energy of the system (kinetic plus gravitational potential) can be calculated at any point on that cycle.

**Stability** is then defined as the time constant for the system's energy to return to its nominal limit-cycle energy (E₀) after the motor injects a perturbation. A shorter time constant indicates a more stable system. **Agility** is defined using the same energy framework but in a different direction: instead of being knocked off the limit cycle by a perturbation, the participant is given a new target (a higher or lower energy level), and agility is quantified by how quickly the system reaches the new target. A shorter transition time, or equivalently a higher average power over the transition, indicates greater agility. This approach uses a common energy currency, making it possible to compare the costs and timescales of stabilization, agile transitions, and metabolic efficiency within one framework.
